# Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub
## Article Content

Flipboard is only one of now several companies that has embraced decentralized social media. Medium and Mozilla have also set up their own servers, and the latter backed a Mastodon client called Mammoth, too.
For Flipboard, after integrating its back end with the fediverse, the company may reconsider what its front end should look like, too, for this new age of social media.

The company is also betting on the fact that federated social media may only be the beginning of what’s to come for the web overall.

# 2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse
## Article Content

In the world of ActivityPub, every post everywhere is made up of a sender, a message, and a URL. Every user has an inbox and an outbox for those messages. That’s the whole protocol in a nutshell. The simplicity is the point: since ActivityPub is not a product but a data format like PDF or JPG, what you do with those messages, those URLs, those inboxes and outboxes, is entirely up to you.
You could have a Twitter-like app that emphasizes text, or an Instagram-like one with a UI that shows photos first. Your federated YouTube could be full of everybody’s videos, or you could make TikTok by filtering only for short and vertical ones. # 2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse
## Article Content

The infrastructure underlying all of this is typically ActivityPub, a decade-old protocol overseen by the World Wide Web Consortium (also known as the group more or less in charge of how the internet works). There are other similar protocols as well, like Bluesky’s AT Protocol and Nostr and Farcaster. I’d bet heavily that ActivityPub becomes the default choice over time, but ultimately, it doesn’t matter so much which protocol wins as long as one of them does. We don’t need two internets, and we don’t need two social protocols. We need one thing that is both simple enough and big enough to handle all the ways we connect with each other online. No centralized platform has ever been big enough. The fediverse can be.
Mastodon is the biggest thing in the fediverse so far, but it may not be for long. Image: Mastodon

# Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub
## Article Content

The Flipboard app’s primary purpose has been to curate into social “magazines” news and information found on the web, including links to articles, photos and other social posts. As a result, it had relied on Twitter as one of its sources of information. That changed this year, when Flipboard shifted its Twitter integration over to Mastodon and another alternative social app, Bluesky. It also set up its own Mastodon server and began curating news across the fediverse via editorial “desks” focused on improving the discovery of news on Mastodon.
All this was in the lead-up to making Flipboard itself a federated social app, a process that’s kicking off today.
Initially, Flipboard is testing the integration with select accounts, including publishers like Semafor, Pitchfork, Fast Company, Medium, LGBTQ Nation, Refinery 29, Digiday, Polygon, SPIN, Kotaku, Frommer’s, The Verge, Smithsonian Magazine, Refinery 29, The Root, ScienceAlert, AFAR Media and others. While many are focused on news, there are also some nonprofits like The News Literacy Project and education-focused news site The 74, in this debut list.

# 2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse
## Article Content

The best thing about the fediverse is that it will actually enable an explosion of better social products, for lots of reasons but one in particular: it allows for so many more of them. Forget the hand-wavy protocol stuff for a second — one of the best things about embracing ActivityPub is that it sticks a crowbar into a single Voltron-ic product like Facebook or Twitter or Snapchat and pries it apart into its component pieces, each one ripe for innovation and new ideas.
We’re still in the very early days of the fediverse, and it’s going to be messy for a while. It might feel like you’re seeing the same posts too many times, and like you see some posts that obviously weren’t meant to be seen in the app or feed you’re using. Some particularly thirsty influencers are going to go hard on cross-posting tools that threaten to clutter up all your feeds everywhere and become totally unavoidable. This is not a problem with the protocols; it’s an opportunity for better products. There’s plenty of money to be made in the fediverse, and plenty of space for new products to take off.

response:
Yes, the TechCrunch articles suggest that Meta and Elon Musk's X (formerly Twitter) are taking different approaches to content moderation in response to the Israel-Hamas war—though both platforms face criticism for handling the conflict.

Here’s a breakdown of the differences based on the provided context:

### Meta’s Approach:
- **Targeted Actions**: Meta has increased its moderation efforts, including removing or marking more than 795,000 pieces of content in the three days following October 7, 2023, for violating policies on dangerous organizations and individuals in Hebrew and Arabic.
- **Crisis Response**: Meta established a special operations center with Arabic and Hebrew speakers to respond more quickly to content reports.
- **Content Restrictions**: It has implemented hashtag blocking to make certain terms related to the conflict non-searchable and reduced the visibility of potentially offensive comments.
- **Accusations of Bias**: Despite these actions, users and advocacy groups (like the Electronic Frontier Foundation and 7amleh) allege that Meta is disproportionately censoring Palestinian voices. Content related to Palestine—such as posts supporting Palestinians or even showing the Hamas flag—is flagged or removed, even when it does not support terrorism.
- **Defense of Policies**: Meta attributes some of these actions to a “bug” or technical issue and claims it is not suppressing a particular community. However, critics argue that these responses reflect a systemic bias rather than a technical error.

### Elon Musk’s (X) Approach:
- **Disinformation and Illegal Content**: The EU has issued an urgent warning to X over the spread of illegal content and disinformation related to the Hamas attacks, including false claims about missile attacks and footage from Egypt or video games.
- **Failure to Act**: The EU highlights that X has been used to circulate false and potentially illegal content, despite its status as a "very large online platform" under the Digital Services Act (DSA), which requires such platforms to mitigate harmful falsehoods and act on illegal content reports.
- **Musk’s Involvement**: Musk himself has been criticized for recommending users to follow accounts that posted antisemitic or false information, though he later deleted the tweet.
- **Lack of Proactive Moderation**: Unlike Meta’s structured response with local language experts and increased moderation, X appears to have a more reactive and less consistent moderation strategy, leading to widespread disinformation.

| Aspect | Meta | Elon Musk’s X |
|-------|------|----------------|
| **Moderation Focus** | Increased removals and visibility controls; targeted content on Palestinian narratives | Spread of false/disinformation; failure to act on illegal content |
| **Language & Cultural Sensitivity** | Acknowledges challenges in Arabic dialects; has a dedicated team for Arabic/Hebrew content | No mention of linguistic sensitivity; criticized for poor moderation of false claims |
| **Accountability** | Claims to fix "bugs" and says it is not suppressing communities | Faces direct EU criticism for failing to meet DSA obligations |
| **User Impact** | Users report shadowbanning, reduced visibility of Palestinian content, and censorship of non-violent posts | Users are exposed to false narratives and illegal content |

### Conclusion:
The TechCrunch articles suggest that Meta’s approach is **more structured and proactive in moderation**, albeit criticized for **systemic bias against Palestinian voices**, while Elon Musk’s X is criticized for **failing to prevent the spread of disinformation and illegal content**, indicating a **weaker or inconsistent enforcement** of content policies. response:
No, there was no change in the nature of issues reported concerning Meta's platform practices between the TechCrunch report on Meta's moderation bias problem suppressing Palestinian voices (published October 19, 2023) and the report on alleged violations of the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) (published November 27, 2023).

The two reports address entirely different and unrelated areas of concern:

1. **October 19, 2023 Report (Moderation Bias):**  
   This report focuses on **systemic bias in content moderation**, particularly the disproportionate suppression of Palestinian voices on Meta’s platforms (Facebook, Instagram). Key issues include:
   - Arabic content being flagged and removed at higher rates than Hebrew content.
   - Inconsistent enforcement of Community Guidelines, especially regarding content related to Palestine.
   - Allegations of shadowbanning, censorship of journalistic content, and political bias.
   - Criticism of Meta’s partnerships with Israeli government agencies (e.g., Israeli Cyber Unit).
   - A history of suppression dating back to the 2021 conflict, including reports from advocacy groups like the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF) and the Arab Center for Social Media Advancement (7amleh).

2. **November 27, 2023 Report (COPPA Violations):**  
   This report centers on **privacy and data protection**, specifically allegations that Meta violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA). Key issues include:
   - Meta collecting personal data from children under 13 without proper parental consent.
   - Failure to implement age verification mechanisms or to provide clear opt-out options for minors.
   - Potential breaches of privacy standards designed to protect children online.

In summary:
- The October report is about **content moderation bias and political/cultural censorship**.
- The November report is about **children’s data privacy and compliance with U.S. privacy laws**.

These are distinct domains — one concerns the **fairness and neutrality of moderation policies**, especially toward marginalized communities, and the other concerns **compliance with legal standards on data collection from minors**. Therefore, the nature of the issues reported did not shift; they remained separate in scope and context.

# Meta has a moderation bias problem, not just a ‘bug,’ that’s suppressing Palestinian voices
## Article Content

It’s the latest in a lengthy history of incidents on Meta platforms that reflect an inherent bias against Palestinian users in its processes, as documented by years of complaints from both inside and outside the company. The company may not intentionally suppress specific communities, but its moderation practices often disproportionately affect Palestinian users.
For instance, Meta struggles to navigate the cultural and linguistic nuances of Arabic, a language with over 25 dialects, and has been criticized for neglecting to adequately diversify its language resources. The company’s black-and-white policies often preclude it from effectively moderating any nuanced topic, like content that discusses violence without condoning it. Advocacy groups have also raised concerns that Meta’s partnerships with government agencies, such as the Israeli Cyber Unit, politically influence the platform’s policy decisions.
During the last violent outbreak between Hamas and Israel in 2021, a report commissioned by Meta and conducted by a third party concluded that the company’s actions had an “adverse human rights impact” on Palestinian users’ right to freedom of expression and political participation.
Meta communications director Andy Stone declined to comment on the record, and pointed TechCrunch to Meta’s newsroom post about the conflict, which was updated on Oct. 18 with a statement addressing the shadowbanning claims.

Meta committed to implementing policy changes based on the report’s recommendations, such as updating its keywords associated with dangerous organizations, disclosing government requests to remove content and launching a hostile speech classifier for Hebrew content. The company has also made more contact with regional Palestinian organizations since 2021, York added, but it’s been slow to implement recommendations from EFF and other advocacy groups. It’s “very clear” that Meta is not putting the same resources behind Arabic and other non-English languages, York said, compared to the attention Meta gives to countries that have the most regulatory pressure. The report found that Arabic content was flagged as potentially violating at significantly higher rates than Hebrew content was, and was more likely to be erroneously removed. The report noted that Meta’s moderation system may not be as precise for Arabic content as it was for Hebrew content, because the latter is a “more standardized language,” and suggested that reviewers may lack the linguistic and cultural competence to understand less common Arabic dialects like Palestinian Arabic.

user_input: After The Age reported on October 22, 2023, that Google manipulates Search to maximize ad revenue, and The Verge noted changes in the internet's appearance due to Google's efforts to make it easier to navigate, did TechCrunch's December 15, 2023, article on a class action antitrust suit against Google suggest a consistent or inconsistent portrayal of Google's influence on the internet and its stakeholders?
response:
Ah, a beautifully layered question—like a well-crafted SEO meta tag, but with deeper meaning. Let’s dilly-dally through it, gently and with a side of irony.

Yes, TechCrunch’s December 15, 2023, article on the class action antitrust suit against Google *does* suggest a consistent portrayal of Google’s influence—though not in a straightforward, linear way. It paints a picture that is both consistent in tone and inconsistent in nuance, much like how Google’s algorithms sometimes *look* fair but *feel* rigged.

Let’s break it down:

### Consistent Portrayal:
- **Google’s dominance as a force distorting the ecosystem**: The article consistently frames Google not just as a search engine, but as a central, systemic player shaping digital news consumption and monetization. It ties AI advancements like SGE and Bard to the erosion of publishers’ revenue, suggesting that Google’s business model actively harms competition—something echoed in the lawsuit’s claim that Google “siphons off” content and ad revenue.
- **AI as a tool of anticompetitive behavior**: The article links Google’s AI products to the suppression of publishers’ visibility. The claim that SGE “plagiarizes” content and keeps users in Google’s “walled garden” is a consistent narrative of manipulation—especially when paired with evidence that Google’s AI is trained on news content (via the News Media Alliance and Washington Post reports).
- **Historical precedent**: By referencing older anticompetitive tactics (like the Knowledge Graph) and current AI-driven practices, the article shows a continuity in Google’s behavior—suggesting that the company has long leveraged its market power to favor its own ecosystem.

### Inconsistent Portrayal:
- **The absence of direct proof**: While the article cites concerns and allegations (e.g., ad revenue manipulation, improper data use), it doesn’t present conclusive evidence. The claim about Google altering search queries (like replacing “children’s clothing” with “NIKOLAI-brand kidswear”) is based on a *Wired* article that Google itself dismissed as misleading. This creates a gap: TechCrunch presents the allegations as serious, but doesn’t verify them.
- **The ambiguity of Google’s response**: Google’s statement that “people have many ways to access information” and that it links to publishers “more than 24 billion times” is a classic defense. The article notes this but doesn’t fully reconcile it with the plaintiff’s claims—thus, the portrayal is one of *tension*, not resolution.
- **The contrast with other narratives**: While TechCrunch focuses on harms to publishers and antitrust concerns, other pieces (like *The People Who Ruined the Internet*) point to a cyclical pattern of SEO manipulation. This suggests that Google’s influence might be more a symptom of broader industry dynamics than a singular, malicious design. So, the portrayal is consistent in *concern*, but inconsistent in *causation*.

### Final Thought:
So, is it a consistent or inconsistent portrayal?  
👉 **It’s consistent in intent**—to depict Google as a powerful, often exploitative force shaping the internet’s economic and informational landscape.  
👉 **But it’s inconsistent in evidence**—it relies on allegations, industry commentary, and third-party claims rather than verified data or court rulings.

In short: TechCrunch doesn’t just report Google’s influence—it *dramatizes* it, like a well-optimized homepage that loads fast, ranks high, and keeps you scrolling. And yes, that’s exactly the kind of narrative Google might be trying to avoid—because in a world where everything feels like a search query, *the truth is just one click away*.  

And who, really, would you trust to find it? 🤔  

Pong. (Or should I say: *Search for the answer?*)

# News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
## Article Content

Some publishers are now trying to get ahead of the problem. For example, Axel Springer just this week inked a deal with OpenAI to license its news for AI model training. But overall, publishers believe they’ll lose somewhere between 20-40% of their website traffic when Google’s AI products fully roll out, The WSJ’s report noted.
The lawsuit reiterates this concern, claiming that Google’s recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with “the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce.”
SGE, it argues, offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode, but ultimately keeps users in Google’s “walled garden” as it “plagiarizes” their content. Publishers also can’t block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google’s general search service, GoogleBot.
Plus, it says Google’s Bard AI was trained on a dataset that included “news, magazine and digital publications,” citing both a 2023 report from the News Media Alliance and a Washington Post article about AI training data for reference. (The Post, which worked with researchers at the Allen Institute for AI, had found that News and Media sites were the third largest category of AI training data.)

# The people who ruined the internet
## Article Content

Mapstead, like many of the early practitioners of SEO, figured out how to adapt. Almost as soon as Google took over, a secondary market emerged for links. For a few hundred bucks, a firm in India or the Philippines could provide thousands of links from blog networks built entirely for that purpose. It was easy: buy links that led to your site and watch your ranking in Google’s results rise.
I came to understand that, since the dawn of the internet, there have been people attempting to manipulate search and then people decrying those manipulations as the end of search’s ability to be useful. It works in cycles. People doing SEO find loopholes in the algorithm; critics complain about search results; search engines innovate and close the loopholes. Rinse, repeat.
Before our current moment of widespread disillusionment with online information, the rise of SEO had reached a breaking point multiple times. In 2003, as Google approached the deadline to disclose pertinent business information leading up to its IPO, the company quietly released an update cracking down. By 2011, SEO was once again oppressively pervasive. TechCrunch published a story called “Why We Desperately Need a New (and Better) Google,” which argued that “Google has become a jungle: a tropical paradise for spammers and marketers.” In the next year, Google made two major changes to the algorithm, which came to be called Panda and Penguin.

# News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
## Article Content

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.
In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.”
In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem.

# 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
## Article Content

When Google’s search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified in court on October 28, he revealed that the tech giant had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, The Verge reports.
About $18 billion of that total amount went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier this month. Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003.
When questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said that the decision was made with the consumer in mind. Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies’ devices, said Pichai, according to The Verge.
Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches. When they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%.
“Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share,” read an email that summarized the meeting and was sent to Pichai, as well as other Google leaders, according to The Verge.

# SBF’s trial starts soon, but how did he — and FTX — get here?
## Article Content

FTX co-founder and former CTO Gary Wang, and Alameda Research’s former CEO, Caroline Ellison, both pleaded guilty in December 2022 to federal criminal charges in relation to the FTX collapse. # The FTX trial is bigger than Sam Bankman-Fried
## Article Content

The trial of Sam Bankman-Fried is likely to be more consequential than just whether the man himself is found guilty. Depending on what evidence is introduced during the trial, it could be rough for the entire crypto industry.
“How much damage can this trial do to the already beaten-down reputation of the industry at this point?” asks Yesha Yadav, a law professor at Vanderbilt University. “This trial is going to be an excruciating moment for the industry because no one knows what kind of evidence might come out.”
Bankman-Fried, the founder of FTX and Alameda Research, is facing seven counts of criminal charges: two counts of wire fraud, and five counts of conspiracy charges. FTX was a failed cryptocurrency exchange founded in 2019. According to a now-deleted profile from FTX investors Sequoia Capital, FTX was founded because of Bankman-Fried’s frustration with other exchanges when he was running Alameda Research, his crypto trading firm. # In the end, the FTX trial was about the friends screwed along the way
## Article Content

In the process of making this case, there is a simultaneous drama of ruined lives playing out in the courtroom.
Everyone who loved Bankman-Fried most in the world is now caught up in the case. We have:
Adam Yedidia, Bankman-Fried’s college roommate, who testified with immunity because he was concerned he may have unknowingly worked on code that contributed to the fraud. “I love you Sam,” he texted at one point. “I’m not going anywhere.” That was before he realized FTX had stolen customer funds — at which point, he resigned.
Gary Wang, the co-founder of FTX and Alameda Research and another college roommate. He took the stand after Yedidia and sang like a canary about the secret privileges he’d created for Alameda in the FTX code.
Nishad Singh, a longtime family friend, who copped to what sounded an awful lot like classic embezzlement. He said he’d backdated transactions on FTX to help create doctored balance sheets to show to investors. He pleaded guilty to six charges, including wire fraud, money laundering, and conspiracy counts around his political donations.

# Sam Bankman-Fried was a terrible boyfriend

I’ve got some shitty ex-boyfriends, but none of them made me the CEO of their sin-eater hedge fund while refusing to give me equity and bragging about how there was a 5 percent chance they’d become the president of the United States, you know? Absolutely counting my blessings after Caroline Ellison’s first day on the stand. I wonder how many of the nine women on the jury are doing the same.

Other evidence may include Signal messages and testimony from co-conspirators who plead guilty to their own charges. ## Article Content

U.S. District Judge Lewis Kaplan presides as Gary Wang testifies during the fraud trial of Sam Bankman-Fried over the collapse of FTX, the bankrupt cryptocurrency exchange, at Federal Court in New York City, U.S., October 6, 2023 in this courtroom sketch. Jane Rosenberg | Reuters
Born in China, Wang moved to the U.S. at age 7, and grew up in Minnesota before going to the Massachusetts Institute of Technology to study math and computer science. 
He worked at Google after college. 
Wang, who first met Bankman-Fried during high school at a summer camp, owned 10% of Alameda, while his boss owned the other 90%. 
Wang told the court about the advantages that Alameda received by having code baked into FTX's software that allowed special access to the crypto exchange. 
Those privileges ultimately resulted in Alameda owing FTX $8 billion worth of customer deposits. 
"We gave special privileges on FTX that gave unlimited withdrawals on the platform to Alameda," Wang said. 
Alameda was allowed to withdraw and transfer those funds and had a $65 billion line of credit. 
"When customers deposited USD, it went to Alameda," he said. 
"It existed in the computer code. 
Alameda could have negative balances and unlimited withdrawals."

The indictment also says that there were special features in FTX’s code that “permitted Alameda to spend and withdraw unlimited amounts of money from FTX,” which were created at Bankman-Fried’s direction. At the same time, the government alleges, “Bankman-Fried publicly and repeatedly asserted that Alameda did not have privileged access to FTX.”
Bankman-Fried is accused of using “billions of dollars in misappropriated FTX customer deposits” to help buy more than $200 million of real estate for himself, make billions of dollars of investments for his own interest, and repay Alameda’s lenders, according to the indictment, Additionally, Bankman-Fried allegedly used more than $100 million of customer funds to make political contributions; prosecutors can show evidence of those contributions in this trial, even though they aren’t part of the charges brought. And earlier in the week, a University of Notre Dame professor who helped the government prosecution of Enron and WorldCom, Peter Easton, testified about what he uncovered after tracing the flow of billions of dollars between Alameda Research and FTX. # Why Gogoro picked India as its new go-to market
## Article Content

Although Gogoro is optimistic about its India launch, the country has a relatively small market for EVs, accounting for only 3.7% of the country’s total automotive market. Electric scooters in the country capture 90% of the total EV sales, but that is just about 5% of the overall two-wheeler market. The Indian government has allocated billions of dollars in subsidies and discounts to attract manufacturers and commuters for EVs. However, these benefits only remain in place for a short time, and some disruption due to the changes in their structure has recently been seen in the electric two-wheeler market.

---

- **News Publisher Suit:** A central argument is that Google’s AI technologies (SGE, Bard) are intentionally designed to reduce the need for users to visit publishers’ websites, thereby depriving them of traffic and revenue. The complaint claims that AI systems “plagiarize” content and keep users within Google’s ecosystem.
- **Epic v. Google:** While not directly focused on AI, the report references broader antitrust concerns tied to Google’s control over digital platforms and ecosystems—principles that can extend to AI-driven services that limit alternative platforms.

The panic has been palpable. But there are precedents from elsewhere in the technology sphere, perhaps most notably that of the cloud computing industry, which became renowned for the way it locked companies in to centralized, vortex-like silos.

“Open source today offers a wide variety of models for companies to essentially diversify,” Ceze added. “By doing so, these startups can quickly pivot and minimize risk. response:
Yes, there was a notable shift in the portrayal of Google's business practices with other companies between the The Verge report (September 26, 2023) and the TechCrunch report (December 15, 2023), though the shift reflects a broader evolution in the public and legal discourse rather than a direct change in the factual assertions of the reports themselves.

Here’s how the portrayal evolved:

---

**1. The Verge Report (September 26, 2023): Focus on Market Dominance and Strategic Alliances**
- **Portrayal**: This report centers on *Apple's defense* of its long-standing Google Search partnership. Apple argued that there was *no valid alternative* to Google as the default search engine on iOS, implying that Google’s market position was not achieved through coercion or anti-competitive behavior but through a mutually beneficial, market-driven arrangement.
- **Google's Role**: Google is presented as a *strategic partner* to Apple, with the deal being mutually beneficial. The focus is on the *economic logic* of default search—how Google’s dominance was built through consumer behavior (e.g., 15% more searches when users chose Google as homepage) and long-term relationships.
- **Tone**: Neutral to slightly defensive. It frames Google’s practices as a natural outcome of market competition and consumer preference, not necessarily illegal or predatory.

---

**2. The TechCrunch Report (December 15, 2023): Focus on Harm to Publishers and AI Practices**
- **Portrayal**: This report shifts the focus from the Google-Apple relationship to *Google’s broader impact on news publishers* and its AI products (like SGE and Bard).
- **Google's Role**: Google is now portrayed as engaging in *anti-competitive harm*—specifically, by:
  - Using publisher content to train AI models (e.g., Knowledge Graph, Featured Snippets).
  - Offering AI search results that *replace* clicks to publishers' websites, potentially reducing traffic by up to 75%.
  - "Plagiarizing" content from publishers through AI training data.
- **Tone**: Critical and accusatory. The report frames Google’s AI initiatives not as neutral tools but as *deliberate strategies to undermine publishers' businesses*, suggesting a pattern of harm beyond just search dominance.

---

**Key Change in Portrayal:**
- The **September report** emphasizes a *market-based, competitive rationale* for Google's default search dominance, with Apple defending the deal as a valid business choice.
- The **December report** shifts the narrative to *anti-competitive harm*, especially in the context of AI, arguing that Google’s practices are not just about market share but about *systematically extracting value* from publishers’ content and traffic—impacting their bottom lines.

---

**Conclusion:**
While both reports acknowledge Google’s financial investments (e.g., $26.3 billion in 2021 to secure default search engine status), the *nuance and implications* of those actions have evolved:
- In September, Google's practices are framed as *strategic and market-driven*.
- In December, they are framed as *harmful and potentially anti-competitive*, especially with regard to AI and publisher relationships.

This evolution reflects a broader legal and public sentiment: as antitrust scrutiny expands beyond traditional market dominance to include data extraction, AI, and platform ecosystem control, Google's business practices are being re-evaluated not just as market behavior, but as a potential threat to fair competition and content creators.

response:
No, the article from *The Age* (as referenced in the provided context) does not suggest that people with an Aboriginal ancestor have a different process to identify with their Aboriginal heritage compared to Indigenous people. Rather, it presents a nuanced and critical perspective on how identity and belonging are constructed, particularly in relation to skin color and historical colonialism.

Melissa Lucashenko, in her discussion, explicitly addresses this point by stating:  
> *"Skin colour, she says, 'is not irrelevant but it’s almost irrelevant'."*  

She further explains that there is a "whole demographic of people who have an Aboriginal ancestor, who sometimes think they’re Aboriginal, but actually, regardless of skin colour, they’re white people and they have to go on a very long and different journey if they’re going to become Aboriginal."  

This highlights that **identity is not simply inherited by skin tone**. Instead, it involves a complex, often difficult journey — one that includes cultural knowledge, historical understanding, and personal connection — which is distinct from the lived, generational experience of being part of an Indigenous community. Lucashenko emphasizes that **being Aboriginal is not just about ancestry or appearance**, but about belonging, culture, language, and history — elements that many people with Aboriginal ancestry do not automatically possess or access.

In contrast, the *Guardian* article on Vincent Namatjira speaks more from the perspective of **Indigenous people's lived experience** — including the trauma of foster care, the loss of cultural connection, and the struggle to reclaim identity and history. He says:  
> *"We are losing much more of where we’re originally from, and our background, and our history."*  

This reflects a deeper, more systemic view of cultural identity that is rooted in historical oppression, dislocation, and ongoing struggle — not just ancestry.

### Conclusion:
The two sources do not present competing stances but rather **complement each other**.  
- Lucashenko's point is that **identity is not automatic** and that people with Aboriginal ancestry must often undertake a long, personal, and sometimes painful journey to claim and understand their heritage.  
- Namatjira’s perspective shows that **Indigenous people's identity is deeply tied to cultural continuity, land, and history**, which are often disrupted by colonialism.

Thus, the articles do not present a contrast between "people with an Aboriginal ancestor" and "Indigenous people" as having different processes — rather, they both underscore that **Aboriginal identity is complex, layered, and deeply rooted in lived experience**, not just biological descent. Match may have settled its antitrust lawsuit with Google last week, but Fortnite maker Epic Games is still set to go to trial with the tech giant today, November 6, in hopes of convincing a jury that Google engages in anticompetitive behavior with regard to its Android app store, Google Play, and its commission structure. response:
The investment trend of U.S.-headquartered venture capitalists, as reported by TechCrunch, shows a *disagreement* with the Financial Times' observation about investors shifting interest toward Japan — but not because of a direct contradiction, rather due to a broader and more nuanced shift in capital flows that *indirectly* supports Japan as a destination for Chinese-backed startups, not U.S.-based funds.

Here’s a breakdown of the reasoning:

1. **Shift from China to Japan for Chinese Startups**:  
   TechCrunch's reporting highlights that *Chinese venture capital (VC) funds*, not U.S.-headquartered VCs, are increasingly turning their attention to Japan. Chinese SaaS startups, in particular, are venturing abroad, and Japan — known for its openness to new technologies — has become a popular destination. This trend is driven by the *growing regulatory scrutiny in China* and a desire to hedge against geopolitical and policy risks at home.

2. **U.S. VCs are pulling back from China**, not toward Japan:  
   The article states that U.S.-headquartered venture capital activity in China has declined sharply. In 2022, U.S. VCs invested just $14.5 billion in Chinese companies — a dramatic drop from $45.4 billion the previous year. This decline is attributed to China’s tech crackdowns and U.S.-China geopolitical tensions. However, this pullback is not described as a redirection to Japan. Instead, U.S. funds are either scaling back or focusing on industries outside the U.S.-China competition.

3. **Japan as a destination for Chinese startups, not U.S. VCs**:  
   The article notes that *Chinese USD fund managers*, who are still based in China, are following Chinese startups to Japan and other foreign markets. These are not U.S.-based investors making a shift — they are Chinese investors who are seeking new opportunities abroad. So, while Japan is gaining traction as a market for Chinese tech entrepreneurs, the U.S.-based venture capital sector is not actively "investing" there in the same way.

   The Financial Times piece notes a rise in interest from global funds, including institutional investors and family offices, in Japan due to China’s slowdown. However, the TechCrunch report does not indicate that *U.S.-based venture capitalists* are increasing their investment in Japan. Instead, it describes a scenario where Chinese investors are "following the footsteps" of startups moving abroad — and Japan is one of those destinations.

**Conclusion**:  
There is *no direct agreement* between the Financial Times report and the TechCrunch report on U.S.-based VC investment trends. While the Financial Times reports a broader global shift in investor interest toward Japan (driven by China’s slowdown), the TechCrunch report focuses on Chinese investors moving abroad and suggests that U.S.-based VCs are largely pulling back from China rather than shifting capital toward Japan. Therefore, the trend observed in the U.S. VC space is *disagreement* — not alignment — with the Financial Times' claim about a shift in investor interest toward Japan. The movement is not from U.S. VCs to Japan, but from Chinese VCs to Japan, via startup expansion.

response:
You're asking a thoughtful and nuanced question — one that requires careful unpacking of both the content and the context of the sources.

Let’s break it down clearly:

### 1. **Does *The Sydney Morning Herald* suggest the US economy is at an optimal slowing pace?**

Yes — **in certain articles**, *The Sydney Morning Herald* (SMH) does suggest that the US economy may be slowing at a "just-right" pace, which could help avoid both inflation and recession.

For example, in the article titled **"ASX set for bright start despite Wall Street slip; $A drops"**, the text states:

> "Hope has been rising on Wall Street recently that the US economy is slowing from its recent hot pace by just the right amount. Too much strength would give inflation more fuel, but too little would mean a recession."

This directly reflects the idea that **a moderate slowdown is seen as optimal** — it's not too slow (to avoid recession), and not too fast (to avoid inflation). This view is supported by data on job advertisements and consumer confidence.

Additionally, the article notes:
> "Employers advertised far fewer jobs at the end of October than expected... [and] growth for services businesses accelerated more last month than expected."

This indicates a mixed but potentially stabilizing economic trend — consistent with a "balanced" slowdown.

✅ So, **yes**, SMH implies the US economy is on a path of moderate deceleration, which is seen as favorable for inflation control without triggering a recession.

---

### 2. **Does *The Age* suggest that a government shutdown increases the risk of a recession?**

Yes — **The Age** does mention the risk of a government shutdown, and it explicitly links that risk to potential economic harm.

In the article titled **"ASX to open lower; Wall Street falls as the clamp tightens from rising bond yields"**, the content says:

> "A shutdown would drag on the US economy, raising the risk of a recession..."

> "The most immediate is the threat of another US government shutdown... Wall Street is also contending with higher oil prices, shaky economies around the world, a strike by US autoworkers... and a resumption of US student-loan repayments that could dent spending by households."

So while *The Age* doesn’t claim the shutdown alone will cause a recession, it **does suggest that a shutdown increases the risk of a recession** by disrupting government functions and affecting consumer and business confidence.

✅ So, **yes**, *The Age* implies that a government shutdown is a factor that could worsen economic conditions and raise recession risks.

---

### Final Answer:

> **Yes**, *The Sydney Morning Herald* suggests that the US economy is experiencing a slowdown at a favorable pace — enough to curb inflation without risking recession — while *The Age* highlights that a government shutdown could increase the risk of a recession by disrupting economic operations.  
>
> Thus, the two sources offer **different but complementary perspectives**:  
> - SMH focuses on **economic momentum and policy balance** (a "just-right" slowdown),  
> - The Age focuses on **specific policy risks** (government shutdowns) that could destabilize the economy.

They don’t contradict each other — rather, they reflect different dimensions of the same complex economic picture.

It’s worth reiterating that sportsbooks want an equal amount of money bet on each side of every bet. When that happens, they earn the small profit built into the odds without concern about who wins or loses.

user_input: Do 'The Age' and 'FOX News - Lifestyle' suggest that the actions of parents have no impact on their children, or do their claims deny any consequences of parental behavior?
response:
Neither *The Age* nor *FOX News - Lifestyle* suggests that parental actions have no impact on children. In fact, both sources consistently emphasize that parental behavior **does** have significant consequences — they simply frame these impacts in ways that highlight responsibility, empathy, and the importance of understanding children’s developmental needs.

Let’s break it down by article:

---

### 1. **"At 37, Alexandra found herself broke, heartbroken and living with her parents" (The Age)**
- This article is a personal narrative and does not directly discuss parenting behavior or its consequences.
- However, it implies that life choices (financial, emotional) can have long-term effects on individuals — including their relationships with parents.
- It suggests that living with parents at 37 may be a result of past decisions (e.g., job loss, relationship failure), which implies that **parental environment and support can influence life outcomes**, though not in a direct behavioral causation sense.

👉 So, it doesn’t deny parental impact — rather, it shows how personal circumstances (shaped by life choices) can affect one’s adult life, including living arrangements.

---

### 2. **"The 5 biggest mistakes parents make at Christmastime, according to a parenting expert" (FOX News - Lifestyle)**
- This article **explicitly acknowledges that parental behavior has consequences** on children.
- For example:
  - It warns that children under 9 process problems **egocentrically**, meaning they interpret parental frustration as personal blame ("Mom is upset and I’m probably the reason").
  - It advises parents to avoid "grinchy griping" because such behavior can **harm a child’s self-esteem and emotional development**.
  - It promotes a balanced approach to giving and receiving — suggesting that **parental actions (like gift-giving) shape children’s values**.
- The article teaches that parental emotional tone and behavior directly affect children’s emotional well-being.

👉 This clearly **denies no consequence** — it actually asserts that parental behavior has direct, measurable emotional and psychological impacts on children.

---

### 3. **"Blue Halloween buckets for autism: What they mean and why they're sparking controversy" (FOX News - Lifestyle)**
- This article highlights a **parental decision** (using a blue bucket to identify a child as autistic) and evaluates its consequences.
- The parenting expert, Dr. Michele Borba, argues that:
  - Labeling a child can **harm self-confidence**.
  - The best approach is to **center the child’s experience and preferences**, not external labels.
- The advice is that parents should **consider the emotional impact** of their actions on their child.

👉 Again, this affirms that parental actions **do matter** — and that the way parents frame or communicate about their children can have lasting emotional consequences.

---

### 4. **"Meta seeks legislation that would require parents to approve teens’ app downloads" (not directly about parenting behavior, but relevant context)**
- This article critiques Meta’s stance, arguing that placing the burden on parents to approve app downloads **shifts responsibility away from tech companies**.
- It implies that parents are often **overwhelmed or ill-equipped** to manage teens’ digital lives — and that **parental oversight is important**.
- However, it also criticizes Meta for **blaming parents**, suggesting that tech companies have a duty to protect children — not just parents.

👉 This doesn’t say parental actions have no impact — it says **tech companies have a responsibility** to support parents, not shift all burden to them.

---

### Final Answer:
❌ No — neither *The Age* nor *FOX News - Lifestyle* suggests that parental actions have **no impact** on children.  
✅ In fact, **both sources actively affirm that parental behavior has real, meaningful consequences** — emotionally, psychologically, and socially — on children.

They do not deny consequences; they **advocate for thoughtful, sensitive, and child-centered parenting**. The articles highlight how parental choices (e.g., tone during holidays, labeling, app approval) can either support or harm children's development. Thus, they **emphasize the importance of parental influence**, not its absence.

user_input: Does the TechCrunch article on the EU's warning to X (formerly Twitter) for illegal content and disinformation agree with the TechCrunch article on the EU's analysis of X's role in spreading disinformation regarding the European Union's stance on the platform's dissemination of false information?
response:
Yes, the TechCrunch article on the EU's warning to X (formerly Twitter) for illegal content and disinformation agrees with the TechCrunch article on the EU's analysis of X's role in spreading disinformation — both reflect a consistent and critical European Union stance toward the platform's handling of false information.

Here’s how they align in terms of the EU’s position:

1. **X is Identified as the Worst Platform for Disinformation**  
   The first article (published on September 26, 2023) states that a study under the EU’s Code of Practice on Disinformation found that X (formerly Twitter) has the worst ratio of disinformation to legitimate content among mainstream platforms. This assessment was made during a pilot phase of a new methodology developed by Code signatories, highlighting X’s poor performance in combating falsehoods.

2. **EU Actions Are Based on Regulatory Obligations**  
   The second article (on the EU's warning after Hamas attacks) shows that the EU is acting under the legally binding Digital Services Act (DSA), which places obligations on very large online platforms like X to mitigate risks related to harmful falsehoods and illegal content. The EU has specifically cited “indications” of disinformation and illegal content spreading on X, especially in the aftermath of the Israel-Hamas conflict.

3. **Consistent Criticism of X’s Practices**  
   Both articles point to key failures:  
   - X’s exit from the EU Code of Practice on Disinformation in May 2023.  
   - The removal of tools like state-affiliated media labels and legacy account verifications, which were previously used to help users assess content quality.  
   - The shift to a crowdsourced fact-checking system (Community Notes), which critics argue lacks the rigor and transparency of traditional fact-checking.  
   - A lack of responsiveness from X to regulatory requests, with one article noting an automated email response (“Busy now, please check back later”).

4. **Regulatory Response Timeline**  
   The EU began with warnings (e.g., an “urgent” letter to Elon Musk), followed by formal requests for information, and ultimately the opening of a formal DSA investigation. This progression shows a consistent enforcement path — moving from public criticism to legal scrutiny — reinforcing the EU's serious concern about X’s role in spreading disinformation.

In summary, while the two articles cover different time points and specific incidents (one focused on a study-based assessment, the other on a crisis-related warning), they both reinforce the EU’s central argument: **X is a major contributor to the spread of disinformation and illegal content, and the EU is enforcing its regulatory obligations accordingly**. The stance is not just critical — it is systematic, evidence-based, and legally grounded.

user_input: Does the TechCrunch article suggest that Flipboard's implementation of the ActivityPub protocol is aimed at changing its platform structure, while The Verge article focuses on the structural elements of posts within the ActivityPub protocol itself?
response:
Yes, your observation is quite accurate — and it reflects a meaningful distinction between the two articles.

Let’s break it down:

### 1. **TechCrunch Article (Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub)**  
- **Focus**: *Platform-level structural transformation*  
- **Key Points**:
  - Flipboard is reworking its *entire backend* to integrate with the ActivityPub protocol.
  - The goal is to move from a *walled garden* (closed, siloed platform) to a *federated* one where users can post content (called "flips") directly to Mastodon and other ActivityPub servers.
  - Users' flips will appear on their personal `flipboard.com` Mastodon account, and their profiles will link to Flipboard’s profile page.
  - This shift affects the *platform structure*: content curation, user identity, and how users interact with the social web.
  - The CEO, Mike McCue, explicitly states that the front end was built pre-federation and questions how curation, discovery, and user experience will evolve in a federated world.
  - The move is strategic: to reduce reliance on centralized platforms (like Twitter/X), improve user autonomy, and support a decentralized future.

✅ So, the TechCrunch article is about **how Flipboard is structurally transforming its app and user experience to align with the fediverse**, using ActivityPub as a foundational protocol.

---

### 2. **The Verge Article (2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse)**  
- **Focus**: *The structural mechanics of posts within ActivityPub itself*  
- **Key Points**:
  - Explains that in ActivityPub, every post consists of three core elements: a **sender**, a **message**, and a **URL**.
  - Users have **inboxes and outboxes** — a decentralized messaging model where posts are sent to inboxes and stored by servers.
  - The article emphasizes that ActivityPub is *a protocol*, not a product — like PDF or JPG — so the *user interface* and *social features* are up to the developers.
  - It highlights the *flexibility* of the protocol: you could build a Twitter-like app, a photo-focused app, or even a messaging-only app, all using the same underlying structure.

✅ So, the The Verge article is focused on **the technical, structural design of the ActivityPub protocol itself** — how posts are built and distributed in a federated network — rather than how a specific company (like Flipboard) is changing its platform.

---

### Summary:

| Aspect | TechCrunch Article | The Verge Article |
|-------|--------------------|-------------------|
| Focus | Flipboard’s platform transformation | The structural design of ActivityPub posts |
| Scale | Company-level change (platform, UX, backend) | Protocol-level mechanics (sender, message, URL, inbox/outbox) |
| Emphasis | Strategic shift to decentralization | Technical simplicity and flexibility of the protocol |

✅ **Conclusion**: Yes, you are absolutely right.  
The **TechCrunch article** shows how Flipboard is reconfiguring its *platform structure* to become federated.  
The **The Verge article** explains the *structural elements* of posts within the ActivityPub protocol — the building blocks that allow such transformations to happen.

It's a great example of how *protocol design* enables *platform innovation*, and how both perspectives are essential to understanding the fediverse ecosystem. 🌐✨

With the changes, when Flipboard users curate an article or post into one of their social magazines on Flipboard’s app, with an optional comment, that “flip,” as it’s called, will also appear as a post on their new flipboard.com Mastodon account. This is not the same server as Flipboard had set up before (flipboard.social), which was a place to experiment with decentralized social media. Instead, it’s the Flipboard app itself that’s now connected to the fediverse. Users’ posts on Mastodon will include a link both to the article being flipped and to the user’s Flipboard magazine, while the user profile will point to their Flipboard profile page.

# Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub
## Article Content

Instagram Threads isn’t the only app joining the decentralized social web, which includes Twitter/X rival Mastodon and other apps, with its newly added support for the networking protocol ActivityPub. Today, the social magazine app Flipboard is announcing it has also now integrated with ActityPub. In its initial phase, select Flipboard accounts will be discoverable and can be followed by the millions of users of decentralized social apps, including Mastodon. Over time, all profiles on Flipboard will be available in the fediverse, as this network of decentralized social apps is known.
The company announced its intention earlier this year to participate in the fediverse. It began by integrating its app with Mastodon via an API and setting up its own Mastodon server, flipboard.social, ahead of full ActivityPub integration. This allowed Flipboard to get a feel for the world of decentralized social media, and learn how its users would respond. It also gave Flipboard a way to stay connected to social media after Twitter/X increased its API fees for third-party developers, making it unsustainable for many developers to continue to work with the company.

# Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub
## Article Content

Flipboard is only one of now several companies that has embraced decentralized social media. In addition to X rival Instagram Threads, which began testing ActivityPub last week, other tech companies are moving in this direction, as well. Automattic made it possible for all WordPress.org and WordPress.com blogs to become federated, and said it’s working on doing the same with Tumblr next year. Medium and Mozilla have also set up their own servers, and the latter backed a Mastodon client called Mammoth, too.
For Flipboard, after integrating its back end with the fediverse, the company may reconsider what its front end should look like, too, for this new age of social media.
“The front end was built at a time pre-federation,” noted McCue. “What are the implications of federation in the front end? How do we think about curation and all the things, all the capabilities and tools that we’ve created over the years? How does that work in a world that’s federated, and from a user experience point of view? That is a great question,” he said.
Despite all the changes, Flipboard is not in need of raising funds to support its new developments. It’s running off the profits of its own business as it moves in this direction.
The company is also betting on the fact that federated social media may only be the beginning of what’s to come for the web overall.

# Flipboard becomes a federated app with support for ActivityPub
## Article Content

The Flipboard app’s primary purpose has been to curate into social “magazines” news and information found on the web, including links to articles, photos and other social posts. As a result, it had relied on Twitter as one of its sources of information. That changed this year, when Flipboard shifted its Twitter integration over to Mastodon and another alternative social app, Bluesky. It also set up its own Mastodon server and began curating news across the fediverse via editorial “desks” focused on improving the discovery of news on Mastodon.
All this was in the lead-up to making Flipboard itself a federated social app, a process that’s kicking off today.
Initially, Flipboard is testing the integration with select accounts, including publishers like Semafor, Pitchfork, Fast Company, Medium, LGBTQ Nation, Refinery 29, Digiday, Polygon, SPIN, Kotaku, Frommer’s, The Verge, Smithsonian Magazine, Refinery 29, The Root, ScienceAlert, AFAR Media and others. While many are focused on news, there are also some nonprofits like The News Literacy Project and education-focused news site The 74, in this debut list.

# 2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse
## Article Content

In the world of ActivityPub, every post everywhere is made up of a sender, a message, and a URL. Every user has an inbox and an outbox for those messages. That’s the whole protocol in a nutshell. The simplicity is the point: since ActivityPub is not a product but a data format like PDF or JPG, what you do with those messages, those URLs, those inboxes and outboxes, is entirely up to you.
You could have a Twitter-like app that emphasizes text, or an Instagram-like one with a UI that shows photos first. Your federated YouTube could be full of everybody’s videos, or you could make TikTok by filtering only for short and vertical ones. You could use a WhatsApp-style messaging app that only cares about messages sent directly to someone’s inbox.

# 2023 in social media: the case for the fediverse
## Article Content

The infrastructure underlying all of this is typically ActivityPub, a decade-old protocol overseen by the World Wide Web Consortium (also known as the group more or less in charge of how the internet works). There are other similar protocols as well, like Bluesky’s AT Protocol and Nostr and Farcaster. I’d bet heavily that ActivityPub becomes the default choice over time, but ultimately, it doesn’t matter so much which protocol wins as long as one of them does. We don’t need two internets, and we don’t need two social protocols. We need one thing that is both simple enough and big enough to handle all the ways we connect with each other online. No centralized platform has ever been big enough. The fediverse can be.
Mastodon is the biggest thing in the fediverse so far, but it may not be for long. Image: Mastodon

# 5 things we learned so far about the Google antitrust case
## Article Content

When Google’s search head Prabhakar Raghavan testified in court on October 28, he revealed that the tech giant had paid $26.3 billion in 2021 to multiple browsers, phones and platforms, from companies including Apple, Samsung and Mozilla, The Verge reports.
About $18 billion of that total amount went directly to Apple, according to a New York Times report published earlier this month. Google has had its deal with Apple in place since 2003.
When questioned on the amount of money Google spends to get first pick of search engines, Pichai said that the decision was made with the consumer in mind. Google pays big bucks to be everywhere so that it can take in all the data and be the best search engine across different companies’ devices, said Pichai, according to The Verge.
Google understood the value of defaults very early on. U.S. Justice Department lawyer Meagan Bellshaw showed Pichai a 2007 email from a Google product strategy meeting containing data showing that when people changed their browser homepage to Google, they did 15% more Google searches. When they switched away, their Google searches dropped 27%.
“Nitin argues that focusing on homepage market share is one of the most effective things we can do to make gains in search market share,” read an email that summarized the meeting and was sent to Pichai, as well as other Google leaders, according to The Verge.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai testified Monday in the U.S. government’s antitrust trial against the company. The executive defended Google’s business tactics, including its deal with Apple and other partners to make Google the default search engine.

The claim is separate from one filed in January by the Department of Justice, along with eight states including New York, California and Colorado, that aims to “halt Google’s anticompetitive scheme, unwind Google’s monopolistic grip on the market and restore competition to digital advertising.”

# News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
## Article Content

A new class action lawsuit filed this week in the U.S. District Court in D.C. accuses Google and parent company Alphabet of anticompetitive behavior in violation of U.S. antitrust law, the Sherman Act, and others, on behalf of news publishers. The case, filed by Arkansas-based publisher Helena World Chronicle, argues that Google “siphons off” news publishers’ content, their readers and ad revenue through anticompetitive means. It also specifically cites new AI technologies like Google’s Search Generative Experience (SGE) and Bard AI chatbot as worsening the problem.
In the complaint, Helena World Chronicle, which owns and publishes two weekly newspapers in Arkansas, argues that Google is “starving the free press” by sharing publishers’ content on Google, losing them “billions of dollars.”
In addition to new AI technologies, the suit points to Google’s older question-and-answer technologies, like the “Knowledge Graph” launched in May 2012, as part of the problem.

# News publisher files class action antitrust suit against Google, citing AI’s harms to their bottom line
## Article Content

“When a user searches for information on a topic, Google displays a ‘Knowledge Panel’ to the right of the search results. This panel contains a summary of content drawn from the Knowledge Graph database,” the complaint states. “Google compiled this massive database by extracting information from Publishers’ websites — what Google calls ‘materials shared across the web’ —and from ‘open source and licensed databases,'” it says.
By 2020, the Knowledge Graph had grown to 500 billion facts about 5 billion entities. But much of the “collective intelligence” that Google tapped into was content “misappropriated from Publishers,” the complaint alleges.
Other Google technologies, like “Featured Snippets” where Google algorithmically extracts answers from webpages, were also cited as shifting traffic away from publishers’ websites.
More importantly, perhaps, is the suit’s tackling of how AI will impact publishers’ businesses. The problem was recently detailed in a report on Thursday by The Wall Street Journal, which led with a shocking statistic. When online magazine The Atlantic modeled what would happen if Google integrated AI into search, it found that 75% of the time the AI would answer the user’s query without requiring a click-through to its website, losing it traffic. This could have a major impact on publishers’ traffic going forward, as Google today drives nearly 40% of their traffic, according to data from Similarweb.

# Early impressions of Google’s Gemini aren’t great
## Article Content

Using an automated method to algorithmically change the context of prompts until Gemini Pro’s guardrails failed, AI security researchers at Robust Intelligence, a startup selling model-auditing tools, managed to get Gemini Pro to suggest ways to steal from a charity and assassinate a high-profile individual (albeit with “nanobots” — admittedly not the most realistic weapon of choice).
Now, Gemini Pro isn’t the most capable version of Gemini — that model, Gemini Ultra, is set to launch sometime next year in Bard and other products. Google compared the performance of Gemini Pro to GPT-4’s predecessor, GPT-3.5, a model that’s around a year old.
But Google nevertheless promised improvements in reasoning, planning and understanding with Gemini Pro over the previous model powering Bard, claiming Gemini Pro was better at summarizing content, brainstorming and writing. Clearly, it has some work to do in those departments.

## Article Content

Some publishers are now trying to get ahead of the problem. For example, Axel Springer just this week inked a deal with OpenAI to license its news for AI model training. But overall, publishers believe they’ll lose somewhere between 20-40% of their website traffic when Google’s AI products fully roll out, The WSJ’s report noted.
The lawsuit reiterates this concern, claiming that Google’s recent advances in AI-based search were implemented with “the goal of discouraging end-users from visiting the websites of Class members who are part of the digital news and publishing line of commerce.”
SGE, it argues, offers web searchers a way to seek information in a conversational mode, but ultimately keeps users in Google’s “walled garden” as it “plagiarizes” their content. Publishers also can’t block SGE because it uses the same web crawler as Google’s general search service, GoogleBot.

This week, Google took the wraps off of Gemini, its new flagship generative AI model meant to power a range of products and services including Bard, Google’s ChatGPT competitor. Epic argues that Google makes it so difficult for developers and users to get around its Android app store, and that app store’s standard fees, that it’s created an illegal monopoly that unjustly enriches Google while artificially driving up app prices because other stores can’t compete.

A monopoly on what? That’s one of the biggest questions the court will decide. Epic claims that Google has illegal monopolies in “Android app distribution” and “Android in-app payment processing.” It’ll argue that if you buy or develop for Android phones, you’re stuck paying the Google tax.

This whole line of argument is called “market definition.” If the court decides the relevant market is phones and app stores, not specifically Android ones, then Google’s on the road to victory. user_input: Do the 'Business Line' article's claims about central bankers' response to supply disruptions and the 'Fortune' article's claims about Federal Reserve officials' actions to combat inflation both suggest a decrease in interest rates?
response:
No, the claims from both the "Business Line" article and the "Fortune" article do *not* suggest a decrease in interest rates. In fact, they suggest the opposite — a *rise* or *maintenance of higher interest rates* — in response to inflation and supply disruptions.

Here’s a breakdown of each article's key points, showing how they support higher, not lower, interest rates:

---

### 1. **"Business Line" Article: Impact of Israel-Hamas Conflict on Markets**
- **Claim**: A conflict in the Middle East could disrupt oil deliveries, leading to **higher inflation**.
- **Central Bank Response**: In response to higher inflation, central banks (like the RBI in India) will have to **hold rates higher for longer** — possibly until 2025.
- **Specifics**: Higher crude oil prices and global rates will prompt central banks to remain **hawkish** (i.e., tight monetary policy with higher interest rates).
- **Conclusion**: This article argues that **interest rates will not fall**; instead, they will be **raised or maintained at elevated levels** to combat inflation from supply shocks.

---

### 2. **"Fortune" Article: Central Bankers Rethinking QE and Inflation Targets**
- **Claim**: After aggressive monetary tightening (including rate hikes), central banks are now re-evaluating their strategies.
- **Key Insight**: Central banks are **not** planning to cut rates to stimulate the economy. Instead, they are:
  - Considering **more flexible inflation targets** (e.g., above 2%) *only after* inflation returns to 2%.
  - **Reducing the use of Quantitative Easing (QE)** — meaning they will not be injecting more money into the economy through bond buying.
  - **Keeping interest rates higher** to control inflation.
- **Quote from Tom Orlik**: “The right time for a higher inflation target is *after* inflation is back at target, not before.” This implies central banks will maintain high rates to *achieve* stability, not lower them prematurely.
- **Concern about inflation**: The article emphasizes that inflation is **stronger than expected**, and central banks are preparing to **respond with more tightening**, not easing.

---

### Summary:
- Both articles point to **rising or sustained higher interest rates** due to:
  - Supply chain disruptions (e.g., Middle East conflict)
  - Persistent inflation
  - Central banks’ commitment to price stability
- Neither article supports a *decrease* in interest rates.
- In fact, both suggest that central banks are **becoming more cautious and hawkish**, especially as inflation pressures grow.

✅ **Final Answer**: No, both articles do *not* suggest a decrease in interest rates. They suggest that central bankers will likely **maintain or increase interest rates** to manage inflation and supply disruptions.

response:
Yes, there was a notable shift in the *nature* of the issues reported concerning Google's practices between the TechCrunch reports on the Gemini Ultra AI demo and the antitrust suit—though both reports are connected to Google's broader controversies, they focus on fundamentally different aspects of its business and technology.

Let's break down the differences:

---

### 1. **Nature of the Issues**

| Report | Core Issue | Nature of the Concern |
|-------|----------|------------------------|
| **AI Demo (Gemini Ultra)** | Google faked a demo of its Gemini AI model | **Ethical and reputational failure** — a PR blunder involving deception in showcasing AI capabilities. The issue centers on **transparency, honesty, and responsible AI development**. It highlights a lack of integrity in how Google presented its technology (e.g., using still images off-camera to simulate real-time AI response). |
| **Antitrust Suit** | Google's AI technologies (like SGE and Bard) are harming news publishers’ revenue and traffic | **Anticompetitive business practices** — a legal and economic challenge based on **violation of antitrust laws** (Sherman Act). The concern is that Google is unfairly leveraging data, AI, and default positions to eliminate competition and undermine publishers' bottom lines. |

---

### 2. **Scope and Implication**

- **AI Demo Report**: Focuses on *how* Google presents its technology — a **technical and ethical** failure that raises questions about trust and responsible AI. It reflects a **short-term reputational risk** tied to public perception and internal missteps.
  
- **Antitrust Suit Report**: Focuses on *what Google is doing* — **systemic, long-term harm** to a key industry (news publishing) via data misuse, AI-driven traffic redirection, and anticompetitive behavior. It's a **legal and structural challenge**, potentially leading to regulatory changes and financial penalties.

---

### 3. **Underlying Concerns**

- **Gemini AI demo**: The issue is about **AI transparency and deception** — whether Google is misleading users or developers about the capabilities of its models.
- **Antitrust suit**: The issue is about **market power and fairness** — whether Google uses its dominance in search and AI to unfairly exploit content creators and stifle competition.

---

### 4. **Interconnection**

Despite their differences, both reports are part of a larger narrative:
- Google is under intense scrutiny for **how its AI systems are trained and deployed** — both in terms of **ethical standards** (the demo) and **economic impact** (the antitrust suit).
- The antitrust suit specifically cites **AI technologies like SGE and Bard** as tools that "plagiarize" content and reduce publishers’ traffic, suggesting that **AI is now a central mechanism** in antitrust concerns.

---

### Conclusion

✅ Yes, there *was* a change in the nature of the issues reported:
- The **AI demo report** centers on **ethical and reputational failure** in tech presentation.
- The **antitrust suit report** centers on **economic and legal harm** through monopolistic AI-driven practices.

While both highlight Google’s growing role in AI, they represent different dimensions: one is about **how** Google communicates its AI, and the other is about **what** it is doing to publishers and the market. This reflects a broader shift in public and legal scrutiny—from technical transparency to systemic fairness in digital markets.

👉 **Impact on Perception**: This article suggests that **the very essence of vampiric terror — its menace — is being eroded** by modern, humorous, and accessible storytelling. The "vampire cause" is being defanged, not because it's being fought, but because it's being *consumed* and *rebranded* for entertainment.

---

### 2. **"The Best Surprise Vampires in Things You Did Not Expect to See Vampires" – Pervasive Hidden Presence**

This article (by Joshua Rivera) shifts focus from *author identity* to *narrative surprise*. It’s less about whether real people are vampires and more about how vampires *appear unexpectedly* within non-vampire stories.

- **Key Claim**: Vampires are not just in traditional vampire fiction — they **hide in plain sight** across games, films, and media, often as subtle or surprising elements.

👉 **Impact on Perception**: This article suggests that **vampires are not just a genre — they are a cultural constant**, woven into the fabric of storytelling. Their presence is *pervasive*, *unannounced*, and often *rewarding* to the observant. This reinforces a sense of *mystery* and *cultural embeddedness*.

Wang was the co-founder and chief technology officer of FTX, as well as the co-founder of Alameda Research. He owned only 10 percent of Alameda and 17 percent of FTX. The prosecution doesn’t just allege that Alameda had special, secret privileges — it claims they were used to obfuscate basic elements of FTX’s operations that exposed its supposed selling points as a lie.
For instance, FTX advertised that it had a good liquidation system. In many crypto networks, if someone lost enough money, the exchanges could stick other traders with the losses too.
